A person's record exists as fragments held across many institutions, each a competent and good-faith custodian of its own part, with no single place where the fragments meet. The institutions are not at fault; record-keeping is exactly what they do well. The failure is structural: the person the data describes can rarely reach the whole, cannot aggregate it, often cannot interpret it once retrieved, and has little control over where it goes next. Crossing a border, a patient must request copies of their own record and frequently cannot read what they receive. Tests are repeated when an earlier result sits in another system, and interactions are missed when no one holds the full medication list. A reasonable question follows: in what operational sense does a person own data they must request and cannot read? This paper argues that the difficulty begins earlier than ownership, at the level of how data is perceived, and that a precise structural account of a health datum determines the architecture any honest system must adopt. We model a datum as five elements: a value, a time, a source, a referent, and a meaning. Three are observed, fixed at the moment of capture: the value, the time it concerns, and the source that produced it. Two are not observed but resolved against an external commons. The meaning of a value is not contained in the value. A lab value of 6.1 is unreadable on its own; resolved against a shared vocabulary it becomes a fasting plasma glucose in mmol/L, from a named analyzer, on a recorded date, for one person, and sits just above the normal range. The referent must likewise be resolved: that a clinic's measurement and a wearable's reading concern one person is an identity judgment made across sources, not a property of any record. From this the central claim follows. Because meaning is derived rather than observed, a value with no resolved meaning is not data but bytes; meaning is what makes bytes into data. Data therefore requires an ontology. The knowledge layer that supplies meaning is not a peer of the personal record; it is the precondition for there being data at all. Two consequences follow. First, meaning is a commons: shared, public, and the property of no individual. A person can own a value and its bindings but cannot own what a clinical concept means. Faithful perception is therefore not a single act of completion but a continuous resolution, in which the observed elements are preserved verbatim while meaning is resolved, and re-resolved, against an evolving public vocabulary. Second, the resolved elements move on a different clock from the observed stream. Observations arrive rapidly and in real time, from an open and growing set of sources admitted through an extensible ingestion layer, so that the set of source types is itself unbounded. Meaning changes more slowly, though the pace of research is narrowing that gap, which raises the cadence at which stored data must be re-resolved to remain current. This reframes what it means to control one's data. We replace the language of ownership with a structural capability set: to access, to aggregate, to resolve, and to govern disclosure. Two of these carry hard limits. Governance cannot extend to meaning: once the commons is open, anyone holding a value can resolve it, so control reduces to control of disclosure, of who receives a binding in the first place, and never of how it is later interpreted. Disclosure further divides by kind. Granting access is revocable: the subject can withdraw it, and the recipient retains only their own assertions, never the subject's data. Transferring a copy beyond the subject's governance is not: copies persist and cannot be recalled, though as meaning accelerates they drift from the canonical interpretation and decay. Resolution carries a quieter limit: an open vocabulary is necessary but not sufficient, because the commons is a very large mapping resource that few can host cheaply or at low latency, so nominal openness can still leave practical resolution concentrated in a few providers. Independence therefore requires open mappings together with a competitive, portable resolution layer, so that the capacity to resolve is not recaptured by the economics of hosting rather than by licence. Aggregation raises the sharpest tension: to gather a person's fragments one must hold the linkage that declares them one person, and a single point of linkage is precisely a centralized re-identification risk. We do not prescribe a resolution; we observe that the tension is real, that several opt-in mechanisms can shift custody toward the subject for those who prefer not to delegate it, and we leave their evaluation out of scope. The architecture is then forced rather than chosen. Meaning, being a public commons, must live in a knowledge layer separate from any personal record and open to all. Personal data must live in an operational layer organized around the referent rather than the encounter, holding the observed elements verbatim while continuously resolving meaning against the commons, under the subject's governance of disclosure. The separation is not a design preference but a consequence of perceiving a datum correctly. We close by noting an existing instance in which this separation occurred in practice: OntoMorph, an attempt at a protocol for healthcare data, intelligence, governance, disclosure, and evolution, whose knowledge commons, HOLON, separated out of it once the implications of this account were taken seriously.
